title: Strangers everywhere (Diognetus 5)
hookLine: Christians marry, eat and live like others, yet live as citizens of heaven
tomorrow: why would a vision show the church as an old woman growing young?

cards: Scroll a stranger's profile and you can usually guess a few things: the team, the music, the city. A man named Diognetus wanted to size up the Christians that way. Who is this God they trust?

Why do they love one another? Someone wrote him an answer, a short letter that never gives its writer's name. And in chapter five, instead of a list of beliefs, the writer describes how Christians actually live.
It starts with a surprise: you can't pick them out of a crowd.

teach.b: Here's the picture, in plain words. Christians aren't set apart by country, or language, or customs. They don't live in cities of their own.
They live in whatever city their lot falls in, and follow the local ways in clothing and food and the rest of ordinary life. They marry like everyone. They have children, and they don't abandon them.
They share their table with others, but not their bed. So far, nothing to see. Then the sentences start folding back on themselves.
They live in their own countries, but as visitors.
Every foreign land is home to them, and every home is a foreign land.
They spend their days on earth, but they are citizens of heaven.
They obey the laws, and their lives go further than the laws ask.
Paul says something close to the Philippians: "For our conversation is in heaven," conversation meaning the whole way a person lives. So the difference isn't walls or costumes.
It's where the deepest belonging lies, and it shows in small things: a table shared, a child kept, a law kept and then some.

how: Christians read the Letter to Diognetus as an early picture of living among neighbors, and some churches read chapter five aloud as a reminder of ordinary faithfulness.

games.why: Diognetus 5 says Christians follow local ways in food and clothing and can't be picked out of a crowd. the difference is where they belong, and it shows in small choices.

practice: Take one ordinary message you'd send today anyway, to a friend, a coworker, a parent, and write it now, a little warmer or more honest than you usually would. Send it if it feels right, and let the rest of the sit be quiet.
